title: What Japan Hid From Its Own People After Midway
fullText: Hashiima, Anchorage, Hiroshima Bay, June 14th, 1942. The fleet is coming home. Ships that left 10 days ago are moving through gray water toward their moorings. From the dock side, they look like any other returning fleet. Iron and paint and signal flags, the mechanical geometry of warships at sea. But something is wrong with the arrival. The men being carried off these vessels are not going to their families. They are not going to dockside cantens, not being released on shore leave. They are going to hospital wards. And when the ward doors close behind them, armed centuries take up position in the corridors. The nurses and orderlys know better than to ask questions. The men in those wards are called in the paperwork, Himitsu Kanja. Secret patients. They cannot receive family visits. They cannot send letters home. They cannot speak to doctors brought in from outside the classified section. Many are badly burned. Many are in shock. Some will take weeks to remember what happened to them. And somewhere beyond those ward walls on every radio in Japan, an announcer's voice is speaking with quiet authority. The Imperial forces, he says, have won a great victory in the Pacific. The men in the wards do not respond to this. They lie in silence. Who were these men? What had they seen? And why was the truth of what they knew burned into their bodies, carried behind their eyes, dangerous enough that the government of Japan chose to make them disappear? The answer runs forward for 3 years, and it costs Japan more than the battle itself ever did. The government was protecting a story it had spent 6 months making true. From December 1941 through the spring of 1942, Japan delivered on nearly every promise. The attack on Pearl Harbor struck the United States Pacific Fleet in its harbor and crippled it in a single morning. Singapore, which the British had called impregnable, fell in two weeks. Hong Kong fell. The Philippines fell. The Dutch East Indies with their oil fields and their rubber fell. In five months, Japan had achieved the conquest of a maritime empire stretching thousands of miles at a cost in blood so low it seemed almost to confirm the ideology that had driven the expansion. The ideology had a name, Yamato Damashi, the Japanese spirit. the conviction that their warriors possessed a quality of will and selflessness that no western army could match. For 6 months, the victories seemed to prove it. The propaganda had not needed to fabricate very much. Reality had done most of the work, but the machine that packaged those victories that turned battlefield dispatches into national mythology had been built long before the first shot was fired. The 1941 revision of Japan's National Mobilization Law eliminated freedom of the press entirely. In February 1942, all newspapers were ordered to merge or cease publication. Editors who survived the consolidation understood the terms of their survival. The Japan Publishers Association agreed to self-screen manuscripts before submission to government sensors. Self-censorship nested inside official censorship, an architecture that required no enforcement because it had become instinct. NHK, the state broadcaster, organized its programming around military success. Daily broadcasts extended beyond news. Educational talks on rationing production campaigns, monthly rebroadcasts of the emperor's declaration of war aired at precisely 11:59 in the morning. Radio listening was organized through neighborhood associations. No one was to be left outside the national message. Receiving unauthorized foreign shortwave broadcasts was a crime. This was not a system that had to scramble when bad news arrived. It was a system already running, already broken to the bit. When Midway happened, the government of Japan did not need to build new machinery. It simply fed the existing machine different material. In the spring of 1942, in a basement in Pearl Harbor called Station Hypo, a team of American naval crypt analysts is doing something that Yamamoto does not know is possible. They are reading his mail. The Imperial Japanese Navy's encrypted message traffic is not impenetrable. American Signals Intelligence has been exploiting lapses in Japanese cryptological procedure to decode up to 90% of JN transmissions. The Japanese are using two cipher systems code named red and purple running concurrently which creates exploitable overlap. A newer code setting JN25B should have been fully rolled out months earlier. It wasn't. That delay gives station hypo additional time to work with familiar patterns. By early 1942, the crypt analysts know that Japan is planning a major offensive operation. They can see it assembling in the traffic, supply orders, ship movements, coordination signals. The target is designated AF. But which installation precisely? The Americans send a test. The base at Midway broadcasts a plain text message reporting a shortage of fresh water. Within days, an intercepted Japanese transmission confirms that AF is short of fresh water. The target is confirmed. Station Hypo gives Admiral Chester Nimttz the date, June 4th or 5th, and the complete order of battle of the attacking force. Nimttz does not wait. He positions three carriers northeast of Midway where the Japanese plan accounts for nothing. Then there are the pre- battle war games. Japanese officers run a full rehearsal of the operation in the weeks before departure. The officer assigned to play the American side does exactly what Nimmits will do. The results of the simulated engagement anticipate nearly point for point what will happen on the morning of June 4th. The game umpire reviews the outcome. He rules it impossible. He restores the Japanese losses and the exercise moves on. Japan has rehearsed its own defeat. It has looked at what could go wrong and decided it couldn't. On the morning of June 4th, 1942, the most powerful carrier strike force in the history of naval warfare moves toward Midway. The men aboard believe they are hunters. They have spent months telegraphing every detail of their plan to an enemy who has spent months preparing their answer. They have been warned in their own commands war room by their own officers. They do not know any of this. The sky over Midway on the morning of June 4th is clear and nearly perfect. The ocean this far out is deep blue and featureless from altitude. And the coral atal sits on the horizon like a white scratch against the water. Vice Admiral Tuichi Nagumo's four fleet carriers, Akagi, Kaga, Soryu, Hiryu, steam in formation, their flight decks alive with aircraft. At 7:00, a radio message arrives from Lieutenant Joy Tomaga, leading the first strike wave back from Midway. There is need for a second attack. Tomaga's planes had hit the island. They had been hit back hard. Marine fighters and anti-aircraft fire struck almost half the 108 plane strike, downing 11 aircraft, damaging 14 more. The island's installations are not neutralized. Nagumo makes his decision. He orders his reserve aircraft. The 107 planes held armed for anti-ship strikes in direct contravention of Yamamoto's standing orders. Rearmed for a second attack on the island, the flight decks fill with planes in mid-transition. Bombs come up from the magazines. Torpedo crews pull their weapons and wait for replacements. Fuel lines run across the deck plates. The ships are busy, laden, organized around the assumption that the only target worth hitting is the atal ahead of them. At 7:28, a search aircraft reports an American surface force. At 8:09, a correction. The force includes what appears to be a carrier. Nagumo orders the rearming stopped. He orders it reversed. The decks are chaos. Half his aircraft in transition, loaded with the wrong weapons, unmoved from the wrong positions. At 10:20 in the morning, American dive bombers come out of the sun. They come from the northeast, where the Japanese plan accounts for nothing. The combat air patrol has been drawn down low, responding to torpedo bomber attacks that have been dying in waves for 2 hours. The altitude is unguarded. Three carriers hit in 5 minutes. Akagi, Kaga, Soryu. The ordinance stacked on their decks. The bombs, the aviation fuel, the weapons in transition begins cooking off. Columns of black smoke rise into the clear sky, visible from 50 mi. The Akagi will burn for 16 hours before Japanese destroyers put her under. Survivors described floating among burning fuel slicks and wreckage, the ocean itself on fire. On the bridge of the Akagi, Nagumo stands near the ship's compass and does not move. His chief of staff, Rear Admiral Rayonoske Kusaka, has to physically take hold of him. has to persuade him then insist that he transfer his flag to the light cruiser Nagara. This man commanded the attack on Pearl Harbor. He stood on this same bridge 6 months ago, watching history open beneath him. Now Kusaka guides him off a burning ship. Nagumo's contemporaries had said it plainly before the battle. Admiral Nishotukahara, who knew him, put it with no softening. He was wholly unfitted by background, training, experience, and interest for command of Japan's carrier force. He had been appointed because of his seniority. And now he is being led across the flight deck of a dying vessel toward a small cruiser toward a flag he will fly over nothing that matters. Hiru survives the morning and launches her own strikes, fatally wounding the American carrier, Yorktown. By late afternoon, Hiru 2 is burning. Four fleet carriers. One day, the fleet turns for home. In the haste of the withdrawal, the men in the water are left where they are, 3,000 of them. The fleet has no time to linger. The ocean takes them and closes over them, and the fleet sails away. and 10 days of silence pass at sea while the country they are returning to has already been told it won. Return to those hospital wards at Hashiima, the guards in the corridors, the nurses under orders they have not been asked to question. The men who cannot write home, cannot name their ships, cannot explain to their families where they are or why the visits are forbidden. It is June 1942 in Japan and outside those walls, the radios are playing victory. The Naval Information Bureau controls what the newspapers print in the last days of June 1942. The announcement appears in the major papers. It reports American losses. It praises Japanese valor. It elevates the Illusion Campaign, a subsidiary operation that sees the American islands of Atu and Kiska, the only occupation of United States territory during the entire war, into the headline event. The diversion at Midway, the papers say, allowed the Navy to win a brilliant victory in the Illusions. Four carriers are not mentioned. 3,000 dead are not counted. No ships are named. No dates specified. The bodies have not been recovered. The retreat was too hasty for that. The survivors are handled systematically. They are told not to speak, told explicitly with the clarity that military authority provides. Tamayichihara, a destroyer commander who was present during the operation, is instructed directly not to discuss what he witnessed with anyone outside his chain of command. Other ship's crews are confined to their vessels. Many ships are diverted to ports outside the home islands specifically to prevent chance encounters with the civilian population. The surviving officers and men of the lost carriers are dispersed, assigned to units in the South Pacific to the island campaigns now grinding in the Solomons and the Bismar Sea. The majority will die there. They will take what they knew with them. Even the language is drafted into service. Retreat is not a permitted word. In 1943, the army will coin a new term tenshin to march elsewhere to describe what happens when Japanese forces are driven from their positions. The vocabulary of failure simply does not exist. The scale of the concealment ran deeper still. Hideki Tojo, prime minister of Japan, simultaneously war minister, the public face of the nation's war effort, was not informed of what happened at Midway for approximately 1 month after the battle. The head of the government did not know. The Imperial Japanese Navy had maintained its institutional secrecy even from its nominal political superior. from the man whose public authority the coverup was ostensibly designed to protect. The army navy rivalry in Imperial Japan was structural and vicious, and it had grown so deep that the navy would rather let the prime minister go on being photographed at victory ceremonies than tell him what had actually happened. This was not a government lying to its people. It was an institution that had become structurally unable to tell the truth to anyone. And then there were the men from the Hiru. 35 sailors from the carrier's engineering section were left for dead when she was abandoned before dawn on June 5th. They made their way topside as the ship went under. Found a boat in the wreckage and set out across the open central Pacific. Two weeks at sea, June in the tropics, temperatures above 90°, no fresh water, no certainty of position or direction. American naval patrols found them. They were recovered. They were questioned. As prisoners of war in the standard way, about Japanese naval capabilities, they answered. The men Japan had been most urgently trying to silence spoke freely to the enemy. What does it cost to lie at this scale? The answer is not primarily moral. It is operational. Japan lost 120 experienced aviators at Midway. Pilots trained before the war in a program of extraordinary rigor. Men with thousands of flight hours who had taken years to produce. The Navy knew this. But because the losses had been smoothed into something the institution could absorb without admitting the magnitude of what had happened, no urgency was created to rebuild the pipeline. Training aircraft remained a low production priority. Flight hours were cut. The cadets who moved through the system in 1942 and 1943 entered combat with a fraction of the hours their American counterparts had logged. In the grinding attrition of the Solomon's campaign, the final cadres of Japan's pre-war elite squadrons were destroyed. What came after them was insufficient. Not because of a shortage of young men, but because the institution had hidden the problem rather than addressed it. The carriers could not be replaced quickly enough. Japanese shipyards would not rebuild the four lost fleet carriers on a unit forunit basis until early 1945. By that point, the United States had commissioned a dozen Essexclass fleet carriers and dozens more light and escort carriers. Japan would possess 18 carriers in total across the entire war. 14 would be lost. The United States would end the war with 29. The arithmetic of industrial production had been running against Japan since the first day. Yamamoto himself had understood this and said so, but the arithmetic of the carrier battle at Midway should have created institutional urgency. Instead, it was concealed and the urgency never came. To its Axis partners, Japan said nothing true. Germany and Italy were planning operations predicated on Japanese naval superiority that no longer existed. When the Axis was defeated at Elmagne in the fall of 1942, Italy asked why the Japanese Navy had failed to cut British supply routes in the Mediterranean. The Axis powers seldom practiced genuine coalition warfare, but Japan had ensured that its partners were fighting their parallel wars in genuine darkness. The institutional culture that produced the coverup continued producing exactly the kinds of decisions that had caused the disaster. A genuine revision of carrier doctrine emerged in late July 1942. A document that finally recognized the aircraft carrier as the centerpiece of naval power. But recognizing doctrine and changing institutional behavior are different things. The same dispersed formations that had left Nagumo's carriers unsupported at Midway appeared again in the Solomons appeared again at Lady Gulf in October 1944. The institution had learned to write different doctrine. It had not learned to think differently. and Yamamoto. On April 18th, 1943, Fleet Admiral Isuroku Yamamoto boards a transport aircraft at Rabal for an inspection tour of forward positions. The route is known, the schedule is known. It is known because American Signals Intelligence has intercepted and decoded his itinerary, the same apparatus, station hypo, and its network that read his Midway plans a year earlier. and handed Nimitz his ambush. 16 American P38 fighters launched from Guadal Canal. Yamamoto had studied at Harvard. He had lived in Washington. He had watched American factories and American ports and American roads and gone home to tell the Japanese government that a war with the United States was a war Japan could not win. He had forced through the Midway operation by threatening resignation, believing early offensive action was Japan's only chance before American production became overwhelming. He had told his subordinates after the defeat that he would take the blame himself and tell the emperor the truth. He was kept in command because removing him would have been an institutional admission. The codereers killed him. The same intelligence that destroyed his fleet at Midway guided the fighters that found his transport over the jungles of Bogenville. The man who designed Pearl Harbor, won 6 months of victories, lost Midway, and died in a war he had told his leaders Japan could not win, was killed by the Americans who had been reading his orders for more than a year. Japan fought on through Guadal Canal, where a campaign meant to be a brief consolidation became a six-month attrition battle that consumed the last cadres of elite naval aviators. Through the Philippine Sea, where what remained of Japanese carrier air power was destroyed in a single afternoon. through Lee Gulf where the last major fleet action in history ended with the JN shattered and incapable of putting a coherent force to sea. It fought on a foundation of managed lies. The structure had been built at midway and it did not come apart easily. By 1944, only 34 magazines remained in publication across Japan. By 1945, only one newspaper was permitted per prefecture, and even those received only the paper the government chose to release. Japan's public began to understand what had happened in June 1942, only when Saipan fell in the summer of 1944, and the Tojo government collapsed beneath it. By then, the B-29s were already overhead. The carefully constructed narrative of unstoppable Japanese progress had become impossible to maintain. Not because the government chose honesty, but because reality had grown too large to stand in front of. The lie had run for 2 years. Two full years of campaigns, casualties, and strategic decisions built on concealment. The secret patients, the men in the wards at Hashiima, burning and silent while the radios played victory, were dispersed into the South Pacific, assigned to the grinding campaigns in the Solomons and the Bismar Sea, and the majority died in battle there. They took what they knew with them. History cannot fully recover their names. The 3,000 families who waited for word of their sons received no bodies. The fleet had left in haste and few were recovered from the water. There were no ships named in any official notification, no dates given, no locations, no explanation of how the men had died or why or that the battle in which they died had reversed the course of the Pacific War in a single morning. What those families received from the government of Japan was the same answer the government gave its Axis allies, its army, its prime minister, and its own pilot training programs. Silence. That was the only answer. It was the answer for June 1942 and for July and for the two years of campaigns that followed. Their sons went to the Pacific. The fleet came home without them. The country told itself it had won. And the men who had known, the ones who burned and survived and were classified and dispersed and forbidden to speak, went south into the war and were consumed by it. And the truth went with them. And what remained was the paperwork, the wards, the guards, the radios playing outside the walls. Nhìn từ phía bến tàu, họ trông giống như bất kỳ hạm đội nào đang quay trở lại. Sắt sơn và cờ tín hiệu, hình học cơ học của tàu chiến trên biển. Nhưng có điều gì đó không ổn khi đến nơi. Những người đàn ông bị đưa ra khỏi tàu này sẽ không về với gia đình họ. Họ sẽ không đến căng tin bên bến tàu, không được thả khi rời bờ. Họ đang đi đến khu bệnh viện. Và khi cánh cửa phòng bệnh đóng lại sau lưng họ, thế kỷ vũ trang chiếm vị trí trong các hành lang. Các y tá và người phục vụ biết rõ hơn là không nên đặt câu hỏi. Những người đàn ông ở khu đó được gọi trong giấy tờ là Himitsu Kanja. Những bệnh nhân bí mật Họ không thể nhận được các chuyến thăm gia đình. Họ không thể gửi thư về nhà. Họ không thể nói chuyện với các bác sĩ được đưa đến từ bên ngoài khu vực mật. Nhiều người bị bỏng nặng. Nhiều người đang bị sốc. Một số sẽ mất hàng tuần để nhớ lại những gì đã xảy ra với họ. Và đâu đó bên ngoài những bức tường của khu nhà trên mọi đài phát thanh ở Nhật Bản, giọng của một phát thanh viên đang nói với uy quyền thầm lặng. Ông nói, lực lượng Đế quốc đã giành được chiến thắng vĩ đại ở Thái Bình Dương. Những người đàn ông trong phường không trả lời điều này. Họ nằm trong im lặng. Những người đàn ông này là ai? Họ đã nhìn thấy gì? Và tại sao sự thật về những gì họ biết lại bị đốt cháy trong cơ thể họ, mang theo đằng sau đôi mắt của họ, nguy hiểm đến mức chính phủ Nhật Bản chọn làm chúng biến mất? Câu trả lời kéo dài trong 3 năm và khiến Nhật Bản tốn nhiều tiền hơn bản thân trận chiến đã từng làm như vậy. Chính phủ đang bảo vệ một câu chuyện mà họ đã mất 6 tháng để biến thành sự thật. Từ tháng 12 năm 1941 đến mùa xuân năm 1942, Nhật Bản đã thực hiện gần như mọi lời hứa. Cuộc tấn công Trân Châu Cảng đã tấn công Hạm đội Thái Bình Dương của Hoa Kỳ tại bến cảng của nó và làm tê liệt nó chỉ trong một buổi sáng. Singapore, nơi mà người Anh gọi là bất khả xâm phạm, đã thất thủ sau hai tuần. Hồng Kông thất thủ. Philippin thất thủ. Đông Ấn Hà Lan với các mỏ dầu và cao su của họ thất thủ. Trong 5 tháng, Nhật Bản đã chinh phục được một đế chế hàng hải trải dài hàng nghìn người dặm với chi phí bằng máu thấp đến mức dường như gần như đã xác nhận hệ tư tưởng đã thúc đẩy sự mở rộng. Hệ tư tưởng này có tên là Yamato Damashi, tinh thần Nhật Bản. niềm tin rằng các chiến binh của họ sở hữu phẩm chất ý chí và lòng vị tha mà không có quân đội phương Tây có thể sánh được. Trong 6 tháng, những chiến thắng dường như đã chứng minh điều đó. Việc tuyên truyền không cần phải bịa đặt nhiều. Thực tế đã làm được hầu hết công việc, nhưng cỗ máy đã đóng gói những chiến thắng đó đã biến những công văn chiến trường thành thần thoại dân tộc đã được xây dựng từ rất lâu trước phát súng đã được bắn. Việc sửa đổi Luật Huy động Quốc gia của Nhật Bản năm 1941 đã loại bỏ hoàn toàn quyền tự do báo chí. Tháng 2 năm 1942, tất cả các tờ báo được lệnh sáp nhập hoặc ngừng xuất bản. Các biên tập viên sống sót sau quá trình hợp nhất hiểu rõ các điều kiện sống còn của họ. Hiệp hội Nhà xuất bản Nhật Bản đã đồng ý tự sàng lọc các bản thảo trước khi nộp cho cơ quan cảm biến của chính phủ. Tự kiểm duyệt được lồng trong cơ chế kiểm duyệt chính thức, một kiến ​​trúc không cần thực thi vì nó có trở thành bản năng. NHK, đài truyền hình nhà nước, đã tổ chức chương trình xoay quanh thành công quân sự. Chương trình phát sóng hàng ngày mở rộng ra ngoài tin tức. Tọa đàm mang tính giáo dục về chiến dịch sản xuất khẩu phần, phát sóng lại lời tuyên chiến của hoàng đế hàng tháng được phát sóng vào đúng 11:59 sáng. Việc nghe đài được tổ chức thông qua các hiệp hội khu phố. Không ai bị bỏ lại ngoài thông điệp quốc gia. Việc nhận các chương trình phát sóng sóng ngắn nước ngoài trái phép là một tội ác. Đây không phải là một hệ thống phải vật lộn khi có tin xấu. Đó là một hệ thống đang chạy, đã bị hỏng từng chút một. Khi Midway xảy ra, chính phủ Nhật Bản không cần chế tạo máy móc mới. Nó chỉ đơn giản là cung cấp vật liệu khác cho máy hiện có. Vào mùa xuân năm 1942, tại một tầng hầm ở Trân Châu Cảng có tên là Station Hypo, một nhóm các nhà phân tích mật mã của hải quân Mỹ đang làm điều mà Yamamoto không làm biết là có thể. Họ đang đọc thư của anh ấy. Lưu lượng tin nhắn được mã hóa của Hải quân Đế quốc Nhật Bản không phải là không thể xuyên thủng. American Signals Intelligence đã khai thác những sai sót trong quy trình mã hóa của Nhật Bản để giải mã tới 90% số lần truyền JN. Người Nhật đang sử dụng hai hệ thống mật mã có tên là đỏ và tím chạy đồng thời tạo ra sự chồng chéo có thể khai thác được. Cài đặt mã mới hơn JN25B đáng lẽ phải được triển khai đầy đủ từ nhiều tháng trước đó. Không phải vậy. Sự chậm trễ đó giúp trạm giảm thêm thời gian để làm việc với các mẫu quen thuộc. Đến đầu năm 1942, các nhà phân tích mật mã biết rằng Nhật Bản đang lên kế hoạch cho một cuộc tấn công lớn hoạt động. Họ có thể thấy nó tập hợp trong giao thông, đơn hàng cung cấp, chuyển động của tàu, tín hiệu phối hợp. Mục tiêu được chỉ định là AF. Nhưng cài đặt chính xác là gì? Người Mỹ gửi một bài kiểm tra. Căn cứ ở Midway phát đi một tin nhắn văn bản đơn giản báo cáo tình trạng thiếu mới Nước. Trong vòng vài ngày, một đường truyền của Nhật Bản bị chặn xác nhận rằng AF đang thiếu nước ngọt.
